q: The phase of an alternating current refers to the:
o: Angle ωt that fixes its instantaneous value and direction
Root mean square value of the current
Number of cycles completed per second
x: In i = I₀ sin ωt, the angle ωt is the phase; it tells where in the cycle the current is at that instant. Peak and rms are amplitudes, and cycles per second is the frequency.

q: In a purely resistive AC circuit, the current and the voltage are:
o: Out of phase by 90°, current leading
Out of phase by 90°, current lagging
x: In a resistor I = V/R at every instant, so the current rises and falls exactly with the voltage. A 90° difference occurs only with a pure capacitor or inductor.

q: In a series RLC circuit, the voltage across the inductor and the voltage across the capacitor are:
o: 180° out of phase with each other
90° out of phase with each other
45° out of phase with each other
x: The inductor voltage leads the current by 90° and the capacitor voltage lags the current by 90°, so they differ by 180°, which means they are opposite in direction at every instant.

q: Which list of electromagnetic waves is in order of decreasing wavelength?
o: Gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves
Radio waves, infrared, microwaves, visible light, X-rays, ultraviolet, gamma rays
Microwaves, radio waves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, gamma rays, X-rays
Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays
x: Radio waves have the longest wavelengths and gamma rays the shortest, with microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet and X-rays in between. The reversed list is the order of increasing wavelength.

q: For a 50 Hz supply, a phase difference of 90° between current and voltage corresponds to a time difference of:
x: T = 1/50 s = 20 ms, and 90° is a quarter of a cycle, so the delay is 20/4 = 5 ms. 20 ms is one full period and 10 ms is half a period.

q: In an AC circuit containing only a capacitor, the current:
o: Is in phase with the voltage
x: The current is greatest when the capacitor is uncharged and the voltage is zero, so the current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage: it leads by 90° (π/2).

q: The average power consumed over one complete cycle by an ideal (pure) inductor in an AC circuit is:
x: With a 90° phase difference, energy stored in the magnetic field in one quarter cycle is returned to the supply in the next, so the average power is zero. Vrms × Irms is the power for a pure resistor.

q: Which property is the same for all electromagnetic waves travelling in a vacuum?
x: All electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum at c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Their frequencies, wavelengths and photon energies differ across the spectrum.

q: An alternating voltage is v = V₀ sin ωt with V₀ = 200 V. When its phase ωt is 30°, the instantaneous voltage is (sin 30° = 0.5):
x: v = 200 × sin 30° = 200 × 0.5 = 100 V. 173 V uses cos 30° by mistake, and 141 V is the rms value.

q: In an AC circuit containing only an inductor, the current:
o: Is in phase with the voltage
x: The induced back emf opposes changes in current, so the current reaches its peak a quarter cycle after the voltage: it lags by 90°. Current leads in a capacitor, not an inductor.

q: Which electromagnetic radiation has the highest frequency?
x: Gamma rays are at the short-wavelength, high-frequency end of the electromagnetic spectrum. X-rays come next, then ultraviolet; microwaves have much lower frequencies.

q: A capacitor is connected to an AC supply. At the instant when the voltage across it is at its maximum, the current in the circuit is:
x: At peak voltage the capacitor is fully charged and momentarily stops charging, so the current is zero. This quarter-cycle offset is why the current leads the voltage by 90°.

q: An AM (medium-wave) radio station broadcasts at 1 MHz. The wavelength of its waves is (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹):
x: λ = c/f = (3 × 10⁸)/(1 × 10⁶) = 300 m, typical of medium-wave radio. Slipping a power of ten in the MHz conversion gives 30 m or 3000 m.

q: In a pure inductor carrying AC, the voltage across it is greatest when the current is:
o: Passing through zero, because it is changing fastest
x: The voltage across an inductor depends on the rate of change of current (L ΔI/Δt), which is greatest as the current passes through zero. At the current's peak the rate of change, and so the voltage, is zero.

q: Which electromagnetic wave is correctly matched with its use?
x: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone, so they show fractures. Sterilisation uses ultraviolet or gamma rays, cancer treatment uses gamma rays, and remote controls use infrared.

q: In an AC circuit, the voltage is v = V₀ sin ωt and the current is i = I₀ sin(ωt + π/2). This shows that:
o: The current lags the voltage by 90°, as in a pure inductor
The current and voltage are in phase, as in a pure resistor
The current leads the voltage by 180°
The current leads the voltage by 90°, as in a pure capacitor
x: The phase of the current is greater by π/2 (90°), so the current reaches each stage of its cycle a quarter period before the voltage: it leads. This is the behaviour of a pure capacitor.

q: The approximate wavelength range of visible light is:
x: Visible light runs from about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). Wavelengths of a few nanometres are ultraviolet or X-rays, and hundreds of micrometres to millimetres are far infrared or microwaves.

q: The mains supply has an rms voltage of 220 V. Its peak voltage is about (√2 ≈ 1.41):
x: V₀ = √2 × Vrms = 1.41 × 220 ≈ 311 V. Dividing by √2 instead gives about 156 V; doubling gives 440 V.

q: A sinusoidal alternating voltage has an rms value of 10 V. Its peak-to-peak value is:
x: Peak V₀ = √2 × 10 = 10√2 V, and peak-to-peak = 2V₀ = 20√2 V (about 28 V). Stopping at the peak gives 10√2 V.

q: An alternating current is given by i = 5 sin(100πt) A, with t in seconds. Its frequency is:
x: Comparing with i = I₀ sin ωt, ω = 100π rad s⁻¹ and f = ω/(2π) = 50 Hz. Taking ω as the frequency gives about 314 Hz; dividing by π only gives 100 Hz.

q: A heater of resistance 110 Ω is connected to the 220 V rms mains. The average power it uses is:
x: Average power uses rms values: P = Vrms²/R = 220²/110 = 48400/110 = 440 W. Using the peak voltage (√2 × 220) in V²/R gives 880 W.

q: A 50 Hz alternating voltage is v = V₀ sin ωt. Starting from zero, the shortest time it takes to reach half its peak value is (sin 30° = 0.5):
x: sin ωt = 0.5 at ωt = 30° = 1/12 of a cycle, so t = T/12 = (1/50)/12 = 1/600 s. Taking 60° (T/6) gives 1/300 s.

q: For a sinusoidal current of peak value I₀, the mean value of i and the mean value of i² over one complete cycle are:
x: Positive and negative halves cancel, so the mean of i is zero; i² is never negative and its mean is I₀²/2, which is why Irms = √(I₀²/2) = I₀/√2. I₀/√2 is the rms value, not the mean.

q: An inductor of inductance (0.2/π) H with negligible resistance is connected to a 50 Hz supply. Its reactance is:
x: XL = 2πfL = 2π × 50 × 0.2/π = 20 Ω. Leaving out the 2 gives 10 Ω; using fL alone gives (10/π) Ω.

q: A capacitor of capacitance (100/π) μF is connected to a 200 V rms, 50 Hz supply. The rms current is:
x: XC = 1/(2πfC) = 1/(2π × 50 × 100 × 10⁻⁶/π) = 1/0.01 = 100 Ω, so I = V/XC = 200/100 = 2 A. Dropping the 2 in 2πf makes XC = 200 Ω and gives 1 A.

q: The frequency of the supply to an inductor and, separately, to a capacitor is doubled. The reactance of the inductor and the reactance of the capacitor become, respectively:
x: XL = 2πfL is proportional to f, so it doubles; XC = 1/(2πfC) is inversely proportional to f, so it halves. Swapping the two rules gives the reverse pair.

q: A resistor of 6 Ω is in series with a pure inductor of reactance 8 Ω. The impedance of the circuit is:
x: Z = √(R² + XL²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 Ω. Adding R and XL directly gives 14 Ω, which ignores the 90° phase difference.

q: A series circuit has R = 40 Ω, XL = 80 Ω and XC = 50 Ω. Its impedance is:
x: Z = √(R² + (XL − XC)²) = √(40² + 30²) = √2500 = 50 Ω. Adding all three gives 170 Ω; R + XL − XC = 70 Ω forgets that R and the net reactance add at right angles.

q: A series LC circuit has L = (1/π) H and C = (1/π) μF. Its resonant frequency is:
x: f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)); LC = 10⁻⁶/π², so √(LC) = 10⁻³/π and 2π√(LC) = 2 × 10⁻³ s, giving f₀ = 500 Hz. Leaving out the 2 gives 1000 Hz.

q: When a series RLC circuit is at resonance:
o: its current lags the voltage by 90°
its impedance is least and equals R
x: At resonance XL = XC, so the reactances cancel, Z = R (its least value), the current is greatest and it is in phase with the voltage. Greatest impedance is the parallel resonant circuit.

q: A 30 Ω resistor is in series with a capacitor of reactance 40 Ω across a 100 V rms AC supply. The average power used by the circuit is:
x: Z = √(30² + 40²) = 50 Ω, I = 100/50 = 2 A, and only the resistor uses power: P = I²R = 4 × 30 = 120 W (also VI cos φ = 100 × 2 × 0.6). Taking P = VI gives 200 W; I²XC gives 160 W.

q: A series LC circuit resonates at frequency f. If the capacitance is made four times as large with the same inductor, the new resonant frequency is:
x: f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) is proportional to 1/√C. Making C four times as large divides f₀ by √4 = 2. Forgetting the square root gives f/4.

q: At resonance, a parallel LC circuit connected to an AC supply has:
o: minimum impedance, so the supply current is greatest
maximum impedance, so the supply current is least
an impedance equal to the inductive reactance
x: In a parallel resonant circuit the branch currents in L and C are equal and opposite, so the current from the supply is least and the impedance is greatest. Minimum impedance describes series resonance.

q: In a three-phase AC supply, the three alternating voltages have the same frequency and differ in phase from one another by:
x: The three coils of a three-phase generator are set 120° apart, so the three voltages are 120° (one-third of a cycle) out of phase with each other. 360°/3 = 120°, not 90°.

q: In frequency modulation (FM), the signal (audio) wave changes the carrier wave's:
o: amplitude, while its frequency stays constant
frequency, while its amplitude stays constant
wavelength in vacuum only, with the frequency fixed
x: In FM the carrier's frequency rises and falls with the amplitude of the signal and the carrier's amplitude stays constant. Varying the amplitude is AM (amplitude modulation).
